data.Name: TP-01 | Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-01 Identity / Entra ID Compromise
data.Description: Gather credentials associated with personnel of the target organisation from public, criminal, leaked or previously compromised sources. Why it matters: Identity compromise often starts before direct interaction with the tenant. Credentials associated with technical staff, administrators, consultants and support personnel are especially valuable in a system-integrator/MSP context. Primary assets at risk: Privileged identities, Cloud administrators, Technical consultants, Support personnel. Attack-path stage: Targeting / Reconnaissance. Detection opportunities: Credential exposure monitoring; Authentication telemetry correlated with known leaked identities; Identity Protection risk detections. Defensive considerations: Monitor for credential exposure affecting corporate identities; Prioritise privileged and customer-facing personnel for remediation; Enforce phishing-resistant MFA for high-value identities.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-01 | Generic System Integrator/MSP profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Identity compromise often starts before direct interaction with the tenant. Credentials associated with technical staff, administrators, consultants and support personnel are especially valuable in a system-integrator/MSP context. Scope boundary: TP-01 covers compromise and consolidation of the organisation's own cloud identity plane. Do not treat downstream customer-tenant administration or Partner Center delegated access as part of this record unless the same TTP is later referenced by TP-02/TP-03. Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. This catalogue entry is threat-profile intelligence, not a detection rule and not evidence that the behaviour has occurred.

data.Name: TP-01 | Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-01 Identity / Entra ID Compromise
data.Description: Collect corporate email addresses to build target lists for identity-focused attacks such as phishing, password spraying and impersonation. Why it matters: Email addresses are often predictable and publicly discoverable for professional-services organisations. They enable targeted authentication attacks against Entra ID and Microsoft 365. Primary assets at risk: Employee identities, Privileged identities, Customer-facing staff. Attack-path stage: Targeting / Reconnaissance. Detection opportunities: Monitor high-volume failed authentication attempts across many users; External attack-surface / identity exposure monitoring. Defensive considerations: Minimise unnecessary publication of privileged-user contact details; Use separate privileged identities where appropriate.

data.Name: TP-01 | Gather Victim Identity Information: Employee Names
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-01 Identity / Entra ID Compromise
data.Description: Identify employees, roles and organisational relationships to create believable identity lures and select high-value targets. Why it matters: System integrators expose significant professional information through websites, partner listings, events and social networks. Names can be combined with role information to target administrators and personnel with customer access. Primary assets at risk: Employees, Cloud administrators, Developers, Project managers, Support teams. Attack-path stage: Targeting / Reconnaissance. Detection opportunities: Monitor impersonation reports and targeted social-engineering patterns. Defensive considerations: Security awareness focused on role-targeted social engineering; Reduce unnecessary disclosure of privileged-role information.

data.Name: TP-01 | Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-01 Identity / Entra ID Compromise
data.Description: Identify personnel likely to hold administrative, support, finance, security, development or customer-access roles. Why it matters: For a system integrator, role discovery can reveal identities capable of administering Entra ID, Azure subscriptions, customer tenants, CI/CD platforms or managed services. This increases the value of highly targeted identity attacks. Primary assets at risk: Privileged identities, Service owners, Customer administrators, Developers, Help desk. Attack-path stage: Targeting / Reconnaissance. Detection opportunities: Threat-intelligence monitoring for targeting of named roles; User-reported social-engineering attempts. Defensive considerations: Avoid public disclosure of unnecessary administrative responsibility; Use role separation and dedicated privileged accounts.

data.Name: TP-01 | Phishing for Information: Spearphishing Service
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-01 Identity / Entra ID Compromise
data.Description: Use third-party messaging or social services to elicit credentials, MFA information, organisational details or other identity-related information. Why it matters: Consultants and technical personnel communicate through multiple channels and may receive believable messages from customers, recruiters, partners or support personnel. This can bypass enterprise email controls. Primary assets at risk: Employee identities, Privileged identities, Customer-facing consultants. Attack-path stage: Credential Acquisition. Detection opportunities: User reports; CASB/SaaS telemetry where available; Correlation of suspicious messages with subsequent sign-in anomalies. Defensive considerations: Train users to validate unusual requests received through non-corporate channels; Prefer verified support and administrative channels.

data.Name: TP-01 | Phishing for Information: Spearphishing Link
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-01 Identity / Entra ID Compromise
data.Description: Send a targeted link intended to capture credentials, authentication information or other actionable identity data. Why it matters: Credential-harvesting and adversary-in-the-middle flows are directly relevant to Entra ID environments because the attacker may seek not only passwords but authenticated sessions and tokens. Primary assets at risk: Employee identities, Privileged identities, Microsoft 365 identities. Attack-path stage: Credential Acquisition. Detection opportunities: Defender for Office 365 URL telemetry; Entra sign-in anomalies; Identity Protection; User reports. Defensive considerations: Use phishing-resistant MFA; Deploy Safe Links / URL protection; Train users to validate Microsoft sign-in URLs.

data.Name: TP-01 | Phishing for Information: Spearphishing Voice
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-01 Identity / Entra ID Compromise
data.Description: Use voice calls or callback phishing to persuade users or support personnel to disclose credentials, approve authentication, alter MFA, or authorise access. Why it matters: Help-desk and privileged-user impersonation is particularly relevant for service organisations. Attackers may exploit urgency, customer context or internal support pretexts. Primary assets at risk: Help desk, Privileged users, Customer-facing personnel, Executives. Attack-path stage: Credential Acquisition. Detection opportunities: Help-desk audit trails; MFA-method changes correlated with support interactions; User reports. Defensive considerations: Strong identity-verification process for help-desk actions; No MFA reset or privileged change based solely on caller assertions.

data.Description: Acquire OAuth/application access or refresh tokens that can be used to access cloud and SaaS resources without the user's password. Detection opportunities: OAuth consent events; Token use from abnormal clients/IPs; Cloud API audit events. Defensive considerations: Restrict user consent; Audit OAuth apps; Least privilege for apps and managed identities; Protect CI/CD secrets.

data.Description: Use legitimate Partner Center, Entra, Azure or Microsoft 365 dashboards to inspect customer relationships, roles, subscriptions, services and administrative options. Detection opportunities: Privileged portal access from unfamiliar device/location; Unusual navigation/customer access pattern. Defensive considerations: Conditional Access for admin portals; Managed admin devices; PIM; User risk controls.

data.Name: TP-02 | Command and Scripting Interpreter: Cloud API

data.Description: Use Microsoft Graph, Azure APIs, Partner Center APIs, CLI, PowerShell or SDKs with the compromised partner identity or token. Programmatic access increases scale and can allow rapid enumeration or administrative action across relationships available to the partner identity. Detection opportunities: API operation baselining; Unusual client application / user agent; High-volume or multi-customer API sequences. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; Monitor automation identities; Restrict and govern app permissions; PIM.

data.Name: TP-02 | Trusted Relationship
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-02 Partner Center / Delegated Administration Compromise
data.Description: Leverage an existing trusted partner/customer relationship or create/abuse delegated administration relationships to obtain administrative access to a downstream customer. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is the defining ATT&CK technique for TP-02. MITRE explicitly states that in Office 365 an adversary compromising a Microsoft partner or reseller account may leverage existing delegated administrator relationships or send new delegated administrator offers to clients. Microsoft documents GDAP as the mechanism that grants partners granular, time-bound customer workload access. Primary assets / relationships at risk: GDAP relationships, Customer tenant relationships, Delegated administration, Partner Center. Attack-path stage: Exploit Delegated Customer Relationship. Detection opportunities: Monitor creation/change of delegated relationships; Review GDAP role scope/duration; Customer access initiated by unusual partner identity. Defensive considerations: Use GDAP rather than broad legacy delegation; Minimum roles and duration; Customer approval; Regular relationship review.

data.Name: TP-03 | Trusted Relationship
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Abuse an existing supplier, system-integrator, MSP, delegated administration or other trusted third-party relationship to gain access to a downstream customer environment. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is the defining technique for TP-03. A system integrator may legitimately hold customer accounts, GDAP relationships, VPN access, support identities, service accounts or other trusted administration paths. If the integrator or one of those identities is compromised, the attacker may inherit a route that receives less scrutiny than ordinary external access. Applicability: Core. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Customer tenant, Customer cloud subscriptions, Delegated administration relationships, Managed-service access paths, Customer privileged identities. data.Description: Use legitimate external remote-access services such as VPN, Citrix, externally reachable WinRM/VNC or similar customer access mechanisms with compromised supplier or customer credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: System integrators frequently receive customer-specific remote access. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Customer VPN, Remote access gateways, Support infrastructure, Internal customer resources. Attack-path stage: Customer Entry. Defensive considerations: MFA; Named accounts instead of shared accounts; Source restrictions; Session recording where appropriate; Time-bound enablement; Regular access review.

data.Description: Use a valid customer or delegated cloud identity to access Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft 365, Azure or other SaaS/IaaS resources. Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Least privilege; PIM; Conditional Access; Dedicated privileged identities; Remove inactive customer accounts.

data.Name: TP-03 | Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Use stolen OAuth or application access tokens to interact with customer cloud services and APIs without repeating the normal authentication flow. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A partner or customer access token can represent real delegated permissions. Token use may continue even when the attacker never learns the underlying password and can enable programmatic access to Microsoft Graph, Azure or SaaS APIs. Applicability: Cloud / API. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Customer Microsoft Graph, Azure APIs, M365 APIs, SaaS APIs, Delegated application permissions. Attack-path stage: Customer Authentication Reuse. Detection opportunities: API calls from unusual clients/IPs; Token use after risky sign-in; Programmatic activity by normally interactive users. Defensive considerations: Token revocation during incident response; Continuous Access Evaluation where available; Least privilege; Protect app and automation credentials.

data.Name: TP-03 | Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Replay an authenticated web-session cookie to operate inside customer portals using an already authenticated identity context. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Session theft can bypass fresh password/MFA prompts and may give immediate access to Entra, M365, SaaS or customer administration portals available to the compromised supplier user. Applicability: Cloud / SaaS. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Customer admin portals, Microsoft 365, Entra admin center, SaaS management portals. Attack-path stage: Customer Authentication Reuse. Detection opportunities: Session reuse from new network/device; Unusual portal access immediately after session theft indicators; Impossible or atypical travel. Defensive considerations: Token/session protection; Managed-device requirements; Rapid session revocation; Conditional Access.

data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Use legitimate cloud services with compromised customer or delegated identities to move from the initial administrative foothold into additional customer resources. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: The customer cloud control plane itself becomes the lateral-movement fabric. Detection opportunities: Cross-service activity correlation; New cloud services accessed by supplier identity; Rapid progression from sign-in to privileged resource access. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; Segregated admin identities; PIM; Conditional Access; Customer-side monitoring of supplier identities.

data.Name: TP-03 | Remote Services: Direct Cloud VM Connections
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Use cloud-native console or direct VM connection features such as Azure Serial Console or similar provider-native mechanisms to access customer compute resources. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: An identity with sufficient cloud permissions can sometimes obtain direct privileged access to customer virtual machines without using traditional inbound RDP/SSH paths. This creates a powerful bridge from cloud-control-plane compromise to workload compromise. Applicability: IaaS Customer. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Customer virtual machines, Cloud-native VM management, Privileged workload sessions. Attack-path stage: Customer Workload Pivot. Detection opportunities: Cloud-native console/VM connection events; Direct VM access by unusual partner identity; Console access followed by host commands. Defensive considerations: Restrict who can use direct VM connection methods; PIM; Disable unnecessary console features; Alert on supplier-origin console access.

data.Description: Assign additional Entra, Azure RBAC or other cloud roles to an attacker-controlled or compromised identity inside the customer environment. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A delegated or customer-specific foothold may be narrower than the attacker desires. Detection opportunities: Role assignment and PIM audit; New Owner/Contributor/admin roles; Supplier identity assigning roles outside expected scope. Defensive considerations: PIM; Approval; Least privilege; Alert on privileged assignments; Separate role administrators.

data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Abuse PIM/JIT or another legitimate temporary cloud elevation mechanism available to the compromised customer or partner identity. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Supplier accounts may be intentionally configured as eligible rather than permanently privileged. Detection opportunities: Risky sign-in before PIM activation; Unusual activation time/justification; Supplier identity activating rarely used role. Defensive considerations: Approval; Phishing-resistant MFA; Short activation duration; Alert on unusual supplier PIM use.

Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: If a delegated administrator can manage authentication methods, the attacker may create a customer-side authentication path that remains usable after the partner compromise is identified. Applicability: Entra / IdP Customer. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Customer MFA methods, Privileged users, Authentication policies. Attack-path stage: Customer Authentication Control. Detection opportunities: MFA method changes by partner identity; Reset/register factor followed by new sign-in; MFA disable events. Defensive considerations: Strong help-desk verification; Limit authentication admin roles; Alert on privileged MFA changes.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-03 | Generic System Integrator / MSP customer-side profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: If a delegated administrator can manage authentication methods, the attacker may create a customer-side authentication path that remains usable after the partner compromise is identified. Applicability=Entra / IdP Customer; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-03 starts when the attacker uses a trusted supplier relationship, delegated privilege, customer-specific identity, VPN/support account, RMM path or other authorised customer access to enter or operate inside a downstream customer environment. TP-02 covers compromise of the partner-side Partner Center/GDAP control plane; TP-03 covers customer-side use, discovery, privilege expansion, persistence, credential hunting, collection and selected follow-on actions. Hybrid/AD and workload-specific techniques are intentionally marked conditional because customer architectures vary. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behaviour has occurred.

data.Name: TP-03 | Modify Authentication Process: Conditional Access Policies
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Modify customer Conditional Access policies, exclusions, trusted locations or authentication requirements to permit attacker-controlled access. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A privileged customer foothold can be made durable by excluding a compromised/backdoor identity, weakening MFA/device requirements or creating trusted network conditions. Applicability: Entra / IdP Customer. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Customer Conditional Access, Privileged identities, Trusted locations, Device requirements. Attack-path stage: Customer Access Policy Manipulation. Detection opportunities: Policy modifications by supplier/delegated identity; New exclusions; Trusted locations added before anomalous sign-in. Defensive considerations: Restrict CA administration; PIM; Alert on exclusions and trusted-location changes; Emergency access governance.

data.Name: TP-03 | Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Cloud Log
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Disable, reduce or alter customer cloud logging and audit integrations to hide follow-on actions. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: After entering through a trusted relationship, attackers benefit from suppressing customer visibility before creating persistence, collecting email or changing cloud resources. ATT&CK explicitly covers IaaS, Identity Provider, Office Suite and SaaS cloud logging. Applicability: Cloud / M365 Customer. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Entra/M365 audit, Azure/cloud logs, SIEM integrations, Mailbox auditing. Attack-path stage: Customer Visibility Reduction. Detection opportunities: Logging configuration changes; Unexpected audit gaps; Supplier identity changing diagnostic/export settings. Defensive considerations: Separate log administration; Export logs to protected SIEM; Alert on audit changes; Immutable/independent log retention.

data.Name: TP-03 | Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Search customer files, scripts, deployment packages and configuration for usernames, passwords, API keys or other reusable credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Support and project environments often contain operational documentation and scripts. Credentials discovered there can extend access beyond the supplier account and into applications or infrastructure. Applicability: Hybrid / Cloud Customer. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Config files, Scripts, Deployment artifacts, Shared folders, Project documentation. Attack-path stage: Customer Credential Expansion. Detection opportunities: Bulk file search for credential patterns; Access to sensitive config paths by supplier account. Defensive considerations: Secrets management; Credential scanning; Remove plaintext secrets; Least-privileged file access.

data.Name: TP-03 | Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Search for private keys, certificates and other key material that can authenticate to customer systems or decrypt protected content. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: System integrators routinely interact with certificates, SSH keys and application credentials. Stolen customer key material can create independent access that survives supplier-account remediation. Applicability: Infrastructure Customer. Primary assets/relationships at risk: SSH keys, Certificates, PFX/PEM files, Storage access keys, Code-signing or service certificates. Attack-path stage: Customer Credential Expansion. Detection opportunities: Unexpected access/export of private-key material; Reads of key stores from supplier session. Defensive considerations: HSM/Key Vault; Non-exportable keys where possible; Key rotation; Restrict certificate access.

data.Name: TP-03 | Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Query a cloud instance metadata API from a customer VM or exploit an SSRF path to obtain managed-identity or instance credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Once the trusted relationship leads to workload access, metadata credentials can provide a second cloud identity with permissions different from the original partner user, enabling further movement. Applicability: IaaS Customer. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Managed identities, VM instance credentials, Cloud metadata, Application identity. Attack-path stage: Customer Workload Credential Expansion. Detection opportunities: Unexpected access to metadata endpoints; Metadata access by unusual process; Token use following VM console/session. Defensive considerations: Restrict metadata access; Use hardened metadata service modes; Least privilege for managed identities.

data.Description: Search Teams, Slack, Jira or other communication channels for credentials, API keys, tokens or support secrets shared in messages. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Customer support and project channels may contain operational shortcuts, temporary passwords or sensitive access instructions. Detection opportunities: Bulk message search/export; Supplier identity accessing old/high-volume conversations; Search terms associated with secrets. Defensive considerations: Secrets scanning; User policy/training; Remove credentials from chat; Out-of-band secret exchange.

data.Name: TP-03 | Email Collection: Email Forwarding Rule
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Create mailbox or transport forwarding rules to silently copy customer email to attacker-controlled destinations. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Forwarding can provide ongoing intelligence and persist after the original credential is reset. A sufficiently privileged customer or delegated administrator may be able to configure forwarding at user or organisational scope. Applicability: M365 Customer. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Exchange Online mailboxes, Transport rules, Sensitive communications. Attack-path stage: Customer Mail Persistence / Collection. Detection opportunities: New-InboxRule/Set-InboxRule/transport-rule changes; External forwarding; Hidden or unusual rules. Defensive considerations: Disable unnecessary external forwarding; Audit inbox/transport rules; Alert on forwarding created by admin/supplier identity.

data.Name: TP-03 | Account Access Removal
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-03 Customer Environment Pivot / Trusted Relationship
data.Description: Disable, delete or remove privileges from legitimate customer administrators or supplier responders to delay containment and retain attacker control. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A sufficiently privileged customer foothold may be used to lock out legitimate administrators, especially if the attacker has already created independent persistence. This increases the operational impact of a trusted-relationship compromise. Applicability: Conditional / Impact. Primary assets/relationships at risk: Customer Global Administrators, Security responders, Partner administrators, Emergency access. Attack-path stage: Customer Administrative Lockout. Detection opportunities: Privileged account disable/delete; Bulk role removal; Unexpected password reset or auth-method removal. Defensive considerations: Protected emergency access accounts; Out-of-band recovery; Alert on privileged-user removal; Separate recovery identities.

data.Description: Obtain exposed, leaked or previously stolen credentials associated with administrators, engineers, service accounts or personnel who hold elevated access. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Privileged credentials are disproportionately valuable in system-integrator/MSP environments because a single identity may control internal cloud services, customer environments, support systems, secrets or administrative tooling. Detection opportunities: Credential exposure monitoring; Entra ID Protection leaked-credential detections; Correlate exposed identities with privileged-role inventory. Defensive considerations: Dedicated privileged identities; Phishing-resistant MFA; No credential reuse; Monitor credential exposure.

data.Description: Identify employees likely to hold elevated privileges, operate managed services or administer sensitive systems. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Knowing who manages identity, Azure, M365, networking, CI/CD or customers allows an adversary to focus social engineering on accounts with the greatest blast radius. Detection opportunities: User-reported targeted social engineering; Brand and impersonation monitoring. Defensive considerations: Role separation; Minimise public disclosure of privileged responsibility.

data.Description: Map organisational roles to identify users likely to possess Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, Azure Owner, subscription administrator, domain administrator, service-account management or customer support privileges. Defensive considerations: Maintain privileged-role inventory; Separate privileged accounts from public personas; PIM/JIT.

data.Name: TP-04 | Phishing: Spearphishing Voice
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-04 Privileged Access Compromise
data.Description: Use voice social engineering to persuade privileged users or help-desk staff to disclose credentials, approve authentication, reset MFA or initiate a remote session. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Help desk and support workflows are attractive because they can alter authentication for high-value identities without requiring exploitation of the administrator endpoint. Applicability: Core. Primary privileged assets at risk: Help desk, Privileged users, Service desk processes. Attack-path stage: Acquire Privileged Identity. Detection opportunities: MFA reset audit; Help-desk records; Authentication-method changes after voice interaction. Defensive considerations: Strong identity-verification procedure; No privileged reset based on caller assertion; Phishing-resistant MFA.

data.Name: TP-04 | Brute Force: Password Spraying
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-04 Privileged Access Compromise
data.Description: Attempt common or likely passwords across privileged or administrative identities while limiting attempts per account. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Even a single successful administrator login can provide substantial control. Privileged-account monitoring should therefore treat distributed or low-and-slow spraying as high risk. Applicability: Core. Primary privileged assets at risk: Entra administrators, VPN administrators, Domain administrators, Support accounts. Attack-path stage: Acquire Privileged Credentials. Detection opportunities: SigninLogs / authentication failures; Distributed-source spray detection; Targeting of privileged users. Defensive considerations: MFA; Smart lockout; Password protection; Disable legacy authentication.

data.Name: TP-04 | Brute Force: Credential Stuffing
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-04 Privileged Access Compromise
data.Description: Reuse previously breached username/password pairs against administrative services and cloud identities. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Privileged personnel may have historical credential exposure. Password reuse or weak separation between normal and privileged identities can turn external leaks into administrative compromise. Applicability: Core. Primary privileged assets at risk: Privileged accounts, Administrative portals, VPN/support identities. Attack-path stage: Acquire Privileged Credentials. Detection opportunities: Leaked-credential detections; SigninLogs; Unfamiliar sign-in properties. Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Unique credentials; Credential exposure monitoring.

data.Name: TP-04 | Steal Application Access Token
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-04 Privileged Access Compromise
data.Description: Steal OAuth access tokens, refresh tokens, application tokens or managed-identity tokens that carry privileged permissions. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Privileged cloud operations can be performed programmatically. A stolen token may therefore provide administrator-level API capability even without knowledge of the user's password. Applicability: Core / Cloud. Primary privileged assets at risk: Microsoft Graph tokens, Azure ARM tokens, Service principals, Managed identities, Automation identities. Attack-path stage: Steal Privileged Token. Detection opportunities: Token use from unusual IP/client; API activity inconsistent with normal identity behavior; Unusual managed-identity token use. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; Token revocation; Protect workload credentials; Continuous Access Evaluation where available.

data.Description: Read LSASS memory on a Windows system where privileged users have authenticated to recover reusable credential material. Defensive considerations: Credential Guard; PAW; Prevent admins logging onto lower-trust systems; EDR.

data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-04 Privileged Access Compromise
data.Description: Use a valid privileged cloud identity to perform administrative actions through normal portals, APIs and services. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is the primary execution context for cloud privileged compromise. Legitimate credentials let attacker activity resemble normal administration and inherit all entitlements of the account. Applicability: Core / Cloud. Primary privileged assets at risk: Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, Azure Owner/Contributor, Security administrators, Customer cloud administrators. Attack-path stage: Use Privileged Cloud Account. Detection opportunities: SigninLogs; Privileged action correlation; UEBA; PIM audit; Risk detections. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; PIM/JIT; Phishing-resistant MFA; Dedicated admin accounts; PAW.

data.Name: TP-04 | Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-04 Privileged Access Compromise
data.Description: Replay a stolen authenticated administrator web session. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A valid administrative session can expose high-impact portals immediately and may persist until revoked or constrained, even if the password is changed. Applicability: Core / SaaS. Primary privileged assets at risk: Entra admin center, Azure portal, M365 admin center, Customer portals. Attack-path stage: Use Privileged Web Session. Detection opportunities: New device/IP using existing session; Privileged actions from anomalous session. Defensive considerations: Token protection; Managed admin devices; Session revocation; PAW.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-04 | Generic System Integrator / MSP privileged-access profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. data.Description: Use an NTLM password hash instead of the plaintext password to authenticate as a privileged Windows account. Detection opportunities: NTLM network logons from unusual hosts; Privileged account lateral movement; Defender for Identity. Defensive considerations: Credential Guard; Restrict NTLM; Tiered administration; PAW.

data.Description: Abuse PIM/JIT or similar temporary elevation mechanisms available to the compromised identity. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: An eligible administrator may normally be low privilege until activation. Compromising that identity can still provide a path to Global Administrator, Azure Owner or other high-impact roles during an activation window. Applicability: Core / Cloud. Detection opportunities: Risky sign-in before PIM activation; Rare/unusual activation; Unexpected justification or approval path. Defensive considerations: Approval; Phishing-resistant MFA at activation; Short duration; PIM alerts.

data.Name: TP-04 | Account Manipulation: Additional Local or Domain Groups
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-04 Privileged Access Compromise
data.Description: Add an attacker-controlled account to local administrators, Domain Admins, Remote Desktop Users, VPN-access groups or sudo-capable groups. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: ATT&CK explicitly includes local admin, domain group, RDP and VPN group membership as persistence/escalation patterns. This is highly relevant when support accounts can administer customer or internal systems. Applicability: Endpoint / Hybrid Conditional. Primary privileged assets at risk: Local Administrators, Domain Admins, Remote Desktop Users, VPN groups, sudo/admin groups. Attack-path stage: Expand Windows/Linux Privilege. Detection opportunities: Group membership changes; New admin/RDP/VPN membership after supplier login; Unexpected net/usermod commands. Defensive considerations: PAM/JIT; Alert on privileged group change; Restrict group administration.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-04 | Generic System Integrator / MSP privileged-access profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. data.Description: Add an attacker-controlled SSH public key to a privileged Linux or infrastructure account. data.Description: Use legitimate RMM or remote desktop support software with compromised administrator credentials or operator sessions. Defensive considerations: MFA; Named operators; Session recording; Tie sessions to tickets; Least privilege.

data.Name: TP-04 | Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-04 Privileged Access Compromise
data.Description: Use privileged access to disable or modify endpoint security, EDR, antivirus, monitoring or other security tools. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Security or local administrator rights may allow an adversary to impair controls before credential dumping or broader movement, especially on administrative endpoints and customer workloads. Applicability: Endpoint / Security Admin Conditional. Primary privileged assets at risk: EDR, Antivirus, Security agents, Monitoring tools. Attack-path stage: Disable Security Controls. Detection opportunities: Security-product disable/tamper events; Policy change by privileged account; Agent health degradation. Defensive considerations: Tamper protection; Separate security administration; PIM; Alert on security-control changes.

data.Name: TP-05 | Search Open Websites/Domains: Code Repositories
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Search public or exposed code repositories for credentials, API keys, internal URLs, pipeline definitions, package metadata, developer identities, infrastructure configuration and software weaknesses. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Public repositories are a direct intelligence source for attackers targeting system integrators. They may reveal how software is built, which CI/CD platforms are used, who maintains packages, and whether secrets or customer-specific configuration are exposed. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Reconnaissance. Primary assets at risk: Public GitHub/GitLab/Azure DevOps repositories, Source code, Pipeline YAML, Developer identities, Configuration files. Attack-path stage: Locate Public Development Assets. Detection opportunities: External repository secret scanning; Code exposure monitoring; Alert on accidental public repository creation; Monitor public forks of internal projects. Defensive considerations: Private-by-default repositories; Secret scanning; Repository classification; Prevent public conversion for sensitive repos; Remove customer secrets from code.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Public repositories are a direct intelligence source for attackers targeting system integrators. They may reveal how software is built, which CI/CD platforms are used, who maintains packages, and whether secrets or customer-specific configuration are exposed. Threat-led context: ShinyHunters is documented by MITRE as searching target GitHub repositories for credentials/API keys and source-code weaknesses. Applicability=Core; SupplyChainStage=Reconnaissance; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Name: TP-05 | Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Acquire credentials associated with developers, repository administrators, DevOps engineers, package maintainers and build-system operators. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Developer and DevOps identities often hold access to repositories, CI/CD secrets, artifact registries, cloud deployments and customer projects. Their compromise can bridge identity compromise directly into software supply-chain control. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Reconnaissance. Primary assets at risk: Git identities, Azure DevOps users, GitHub/GitLab accounts, DevOps administrators, Package maintainers. Attack-path stage: Target Developer Credentials. Detection opportunities: Credential exposure monitoring; Identity Protection; Monitor developer credentials in public leaks and repositories. Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Dedicated admin identities; Credential hygiene; No shared developer accounts.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Developer and DevOps identities often hold access to repositories, CI/CD secrets, artifact registries, cloud deployments and customer projects. Their compromise can bridge identity compromise directly into software supply-chain control. Threat-led context: MITRE v19.2 emphasizes credential and identity-token theft in current developer/cloud intrusions. Applicability=Core; SupplyChainStage=Reconnaissance; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Name: TP-05 | Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Identify who controls repositories, package registries, CI/CD infrastructure, service connections, signing keys and releases. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: In decentralised development organisations, each business unit may use different platforms and processes. Attackers benefit from discovering exactly which teams have weak or highly privileged delivery paths. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Map Software Delivery Responsibilities. Primary assets at risk: DevOps administrators, Repository owners, Release managers, Cloud deployment owners, Signing-key custodians. Attack-path stage: Map Software Delivery Responsibilities. Detection opportunities: Threat-intelligence monitoring around named technical roles; Review public org/repository role exposure. Defensive considerations: Document ownership centrally; Separate duties between commit, approval and release; Maintain privileged-role inventory.

Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Least privilege; Repository role governance; PIM/JIT where supported.

data.Name: TP-05 | Steal Application Access Token
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Steal GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, npm, package-registry, OIDC, OAuth, CI/CD runner or cloud access tokens. data.Description: Use stolen application or access tokens to authenticate to repositories, package registries, cloud services or CI/CD APIs. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Token reuse allows an attacker to move from one compromised component to another: for example from a developer identity to GitHub, from GitHub Actions to cloud resources, or from a package registry to additional maintained packages. Attack-path stage: Reuse Stolen CI/CD Token. Detection opportunities: API use from abnormal client/location; Token used outside expected pipeline; Token used to enumerate/publish multiple projects. Defensive considerations: Fine-grained permissions; Short-lived tokens; Workload identity federation; Revoke on suspicious use.

data.Name: TP-05 | External Remote Services
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use VPN or other external remote administration services with compromised developer or DevOps credentials to access self-hosted runners, build hosts or development networks. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Self-hosted CI/CD infrastructure may reside inside trusted networks. Legitimate remote access can therefore turn stolen engineering credentials into direct access to privileged build systems. Applicability: Self-Hosted Runner / Remote Admin Conditional. Software supply-chain stage: Access Developer / Build Infrastructure. Primary assets at risk: VPN, Build networks, Self-hosted runners, Developer jump hosts. Attack-path stage: Access Developer / Build Infrastructure. Detection opportunities: New source/device for developer VPN; Remote access outside expected development windows. Defensive considerations: MFA; Named accounts; Network segmentation; Restrict remote access to build systems.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Self-hosted CI/CD infrastructure may reside inside trusted networks. Legitimate remote access can therefore turn stolen engineering credentials into direct access to privileged build systems. Threat-led context: No actor-specific evidence required for inclusion; technique is included because it is structurally relevant to the scenario. Applicability=Self-Hosted Runner / Remote Admin Conditional; SupplyChainStage=Access Developer / Build Infrastructure; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Name: TP-05 | Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Search and collect source code, commit history, pipeline definitions, secrets, tokens, customer configuration and architecture information from code repositories. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Code repositories are crown-jewel information stores for system integrators. They can reveal vulnerabilities, deployment credentials, customer-specific details and direct mechanisms for software supply-chain manipulation. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Collection / Supply Chain Preparation. Primary assets at risk: Private source code, Git history, Pipeline definitions, Customer code, Deployment manifests, Secrets accidentally committed. Attack-path stage: Access and Mine Source Repositories. Detection opportunities: Bulk clone/download; Search activity for secret-like strings; Rare user accessing many private repositories; Public visibility changes. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; Secret scanning; Branch protection; Repository classification; Monitor mass clone/export.

data.Name: TP-05 | Cloud Infrastructure Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Enumerate cloud compute, runner infrastructure, storage and supporting resources used by software delivery. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Build systems may have privileged network placement or cloud roles. Discovering self-hosted runners and deployment infrastructure can expose a path from source control into production or customer environments. Applicability: Cloud / Self-Hosted Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Discover Build and Runner Infrastructure. Primary assets at risk: Self-hosted runners, Build VMs, Cloud build infrastructure, Runner pools. Attack-path stage: Discover Build and Runner Infrastructure. Detection opportunities: Resource-list operations from developer token; Unusual discovery of runner infrastructure. Defensive considerations: Separate build accounts/subscriptions; Least privilege; Ephemeral runners.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Build systems may have privileged network placement or cloud roles. Discovering self-hosted runners and deployment infrastructure can expose a path from source control into production or customer environments. Threat-led context: No actor-specific evidence required for inclusion; technique is included because it is structurally relevant to the scenario. Applicability=Cloud / Self-Hosted Runner; SupplyChainStage=Discover Build and Runner Infrastructure; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Name: TP-05 | Container and Resource Discovery

data.Description: Enumerate Docker, Kubernetes and container resources used by build, test or deployment workflows. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Modern CI/CD often executes inside containers. Container discovery may reveal mounted secrets, service accounts, registries and internal resources that can be abused for propagation. Applicability: Container / CI/CD. Software supply-chain stage: Discover Containerized Build Environment. Primary assets at risk: Docker, Kubernetes, Container runners, Build pods. Attack-path stage: Discover Containerized Build Environment. Detection opportunities: kubectl/docker enumeration by unexpected pipeline; Runner querying unrelated namespaces. Defensive considerations: Namespace isolation; Ephemeral runners; Least-privileged service accounts; No host Docker socket exposure.

data.Name: TP-05 | File and Directory Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Search developer hosts, runners and build environments for credential files, SSH keys, cloud profiles, package configuration and CI/CD metadata. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Developer environments accumulate configuration for multiple cloud and package ecosystems. File discovery identifies exactly where secrets and tokens can be harvested. Applicability: Core / Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Locate Developer Secrets and Configuration. Primary assets at risk: ~/.git-credentials, Cloud CLI profiles, npm config, SSH directories, Pipeline workspaces, Environment files. Attack-path stage: Locate Developer Secrets and Configuration. Detection opportunities: Access to known credential paths; Recursive file discovery on runner. Defensive considerations: Minimise local secrets; Ephemeral runners; Secret scanning; Credential isolation.

data.Name: TP-05 | Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Search developer hosts, repositories and runners for plaintext API keys, passwords, tokens, cloud profiles, package credentials and service-connection secrets. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is one of the highest-value techniques in TP-05. Decentralised CI/CD and secret-management practices increase the probability that sensitive credentials are stored in configuration files, build workspaces or project-specific tooling. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Credential Access. Primary assets at risk: Credential files, Pipeline workspace, Repository config, Cloud profiles, Package-manager config. Attack-path stage: Harvest DevOps Credentials from Files. Detection opportunities: File access to known secret paths; Secret-scanner findings; Bulk reads of environment/config files. Defensive considerations: Central secrets management; Secret scanning; Short-lived credentials; Ephemeral runners; No plaintext secrets.

data.Description: Search shell history for credentials, tokens, registry passwords or cloud commands containing sensitive arguments. Detection opportunities: Unusual history-file reads; Credential scanning of shell history. Defensive considerations: Disable sensitive command logging where appropriate; Training; Ephemeral runners; Rotate exposed secrets.

data.Name: TP-05 | Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Query cloud metadata services from compromised build VMs or runners to obtain managed-identity or instance credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A self-hosted cloud runner may possess a workload identity with deployment privileges. Metadata-token theft can bridge CI/CD execution into Azure/AWS/GCP production resources. Applicability: Cloud Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Harvest Runner Cloud Identity. Primary assets at risk: Managed identities, Instance roles, Build VMs, Cloud runners. Attack-path stage: Harvest Runner Cloud Identity. Detection opportunities: Metadata access from unusual build process; Runner token used against unrelated cloud services. Defensive considerations: Least-privileged runner identity; Harden metadata access; Ephemeral runners.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: A self-hosted cloud runner may possess a workload identity with deployment privileges. Metadata-token theft can bridge CI/CD execution into Azure/AWS/GCP production resources. Threat-led context: No actor-specific evidence required for inclusion; technique is included because it is structurally relevant to the scenario. Applicability=Cloud Runner; SupplyChainStage=Harvest Runner Cloud Identity; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Description: Query container APIs or orchestrators to obtain secrets, service-account tokens or configuration available to a compromised build container. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: CI/CD pipelines frequently run in Kubernetes or Docker. Over-privileged runner service accounts or exposed container APIs can convert pipeline execution into broader infrastructure access. Applicability: Container CI/CD. Attack-path stage: Harvest Container / Kubernetes Secrets. Detection opportunities: kubectl get secrets from build namespace; Docker socket access; Runner querying unrelated secret objects. Defensive considerations: Least-privileged Kubernetes RBAC; No host Docker socket; Separate namespaces; Ephemeral service accounts.

data.Name: TP-05 | Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Access a developer or DevOps administrator password manager to obtain repository, cloud, customer and service credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Developer vaults may aggregate credentials across internal systems and customer projects. Compromise can therefore expand a single endpoint intrusion into multi-platform supply-chain access. Applicability: Developer Endpoint. Software supply-chain stage: Access Developer Password Vault. Primary assets at risk: Password managers, Developer vaults, Customer credentials. Attack-path stage: Access Developer Password Vault. Detection opportunities: New device/session accessing vault; Bulk vault export; Local vault-database access. Defensive considerations: Enterprise password manager; Hardware-backed MFA; Restrict export; Separate privileged vaults.

data.Name: TP-05 | Credentials from Password Stores: Cloud Secrets Management Stores
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Retrieve build, deployment or application secrets from cloud secret-management stores such as Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or GCP Secret Manager. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Pipelines commonly fetch deployment credentials from secret stores. If the runner or DevOps identity is over-privileged, secret-store access can expose production and customer credentials. Applicability: Core / Cloud. Software supply-chain stage: Harvest CI/CD Secrets from Cloud Secret Stores. Primary assets at risk: Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Pipeline secrets. Attack-path stage: Harvest CI/CD Secrets from Cloud Secret Stores. Detection opportunities: Bulk secret retrieval; Runner/service principal accessing secrets outside expected set; Secret reads after suspicious workflow modification. Defensive considerations: Per-pipeline secret scope; Managed identities; Workload federation; PIM; Alert on bulk secret access.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. data.Name: TP-05 | OS Credential Dumping: Proc Filesystem
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Read Linux process memory through /proc to recover plaintext or short-lived tokens from CI/CD runner worker processes. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Current supply-chain malware has demonstrated that ephemeral CI/CD tokens can be recovered directly from runner memory. This bypasses assumptions that short-lived tokens are safe merely because they are not stored on disk. Applicability: Linux CI/CD Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Extract Tokens from Runner Process Memory. Primary assets at risk: Runner.Worker process, OIDC tokens, GitHub tokens, Package publishing tokens. Attack-path stage: Extract Tokens from Runner Process Memory. Detection opportunities: Reads of /proc/<pid>/mem; ptrace/process-memory access by build script; Runner token used after memory-access anomaly. Defensive considerations: Isolate untrusted workflow code; Ephemeral runners; Restrict ptrace/process memory; No privileged runners.

data.Name: TP-05 | Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Steal client or authentication certificates used by developers, automation or workload identities. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Certificate-backed authentication can provide durable cloud or repository access and may be harder to remediate if inventories and rotation procedures are decentralised. Applicability: Certificate-Based DevOps Conditional. Software supply-chain stage: Steal Developer / Cloud Authentication Certificates. Primary assets at risk: Client certificates, Service-principal certificates, Automation certificates. Attack-path stage: Steal Developer / Cloud Authentication Certificates. Detection opportunities: Certificate export/access; New certificate authentication from unusual source. Defensive considerations: HSM/Key Vault; Non-exportable certificates; Inventory and rapid rotation.

data.Name: TP-05 | Poisoned Pipeline Execution
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Modify CI/CD workflow configuration, referenced scripts, tests, linters, build files or pull-request behavior so attacker-controlled code executes in the trusted pipeline. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is the defining execution technique for TP-05. Pipeline poisoning can leak credentials, execute code on self-hosted runners, modify build output or inject malicious components that are later shipped to customers. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: CI/CD Execution. Primary assets at risk: GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Build scripts, Self-hosted runners. Attack-path stage: Poison CI/CD Pipeline. Detection opportunities: Workflow/config changes; Unexpected pull_request_target or equivalent triggers; Pipeline contacting new external endpoints; Unexpected artifact/secret export. Defensive considerations: Code review for pipeline files; No unreviewed code on privileged runners; Ephemeral isolated runners; Least-privileged pipeline identities.

data.Name: TP-05 | Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript/JScript
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use JavaScript or Node.js lifecycle scripts such as preinstall/postinstall hooks to execute malicious code during package installation or build. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Package ecosystems can automatically execute scripts. Malicious dependency or package modifications can therefore execute on developer machines and CI/CD runners simply because a trusted package is installed or built. Applicability: Node / Package Ecosystem. Software supply-chain stage: Package Execution. Primary assets at risk: npm packages, package.json scripts, Node.js build pipelines, Developer workstations. Attack-path stage: Execute JavaScript / Node Package Scripts. Detection opportunities: Unexpected install scripts; New lifecycle hooks; Package install spawning network/download processes. Defensive considerations: Disable unnecessary lifecycle scripts; Dependency pinning; Package provenance; Review package changes.

data.Name: TP-05 | Container Administration Command
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use kubectl or equivalent container administration commands to read secrets, enumerate workloads or execute actions in Kubernetes environments. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Build systems deployed on Kubernetes often have service accounts and namespace access. Excessive permissions can turn pipeline compromise into cluster compromise. Applicability: Container / Kubernetes CI/CD. Software supply-chain stage: Use Kubernetes / Container Administration. Primary assets at risk: Kubernetes, Build pods, CI namespaces, Cluster secrets. Attack-path stage: Use Kubernetes / Container Administration. Detection opportunities: kubectl get secrets; exec into unrelated workloads; Pipeline service account accessing broad namespaces. Defensive considerations: Least-privileged RBAC; Dedicated CI namespace; Short-lived service accounts; Admission controls.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Build systems deployed on Kubernetes often have service accounts and namespace access. Excessive permissions can turn pipeline compromise into cluster compromise. Applicability=Container / Kubernetes CI/CD; SupplyChainStage=Use Kubernetes / Container Administration; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. data.Name: TP-05 | Event Triggered Execution: Installer Packages
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Insert malicious pre-install, post-install or other installer-package hooks so code executes automatically during package installation. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Installer hooks are a powerful propagation path because downstream developers and pipelines may execute them automatically as part of normal package consumption. Applicability: Package Ecosystem. Software supply-chain stage: Abuse Package Installer Hooks. Primary assets at risk: npm/package installers, Developer endpoints, CI/CD build jobs. Attack-path stage: Abuse Package Installer Hooks. Detection opportunities: New/changed installer lifecycle scripts; Package install performing network access or credential reads. Defensive considerations: Package review; Provenance/signing; Block unexpected lifecycle scripts.

data.Name: TP-05 | Event Triggered Execution: Python Startup Hooks
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Modify Python startup mechanisms such as .pth files to execute attacker code when the Python interpreter starts. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Python startup-hook abuse can persist on developer or self-hosted runner systems and re-execute during normal development or build activity. Applicability: Python Developer / Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Abuse Python Startup Hooks. Primary assets at risk: Python environments, Developer hosts, Self-hosted runners. Attack-path stage: Abuse Python Startup Hooks. Detection opportunities: New/modified .pth files; Python startup network activity; Unexpected code loaded at interpreter launch. Defensive considerations: Immutable/ephemeral runners; File integrity monitoring; Virtual environment hygiene.

data.Name: TP-05 | Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Compromise or replace software dependencies, package-manager content, development tools, IDE extensions, build plugins or CI/CD components so malicious code executes in downstream environments. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: System integrators consume large dependency ecosystems and may publish packages or use common development tools across many projects. A malicious dependency or development tool can compromise internal builds and become a route to customers. Applicability: Core. Software supply-chain stage: Supply Chain Compromise. Primary assets at risk: Open-source dependencies, npm/PyPI/NuGet/Maven packages, IDE extensions, CI/CD actions/plugins, Build tools. Attack-path stage: Compromise Dependency / Development Tool. Detection opportunities: Dependency changes; New maintainers; Unexpected package version/provenance; Malicious install scripts; Integrity changes in development tools. Defensive considerations: Dependency pinning; SBOM; Package provenance/signatures; Private mirrors; Dependency review; Allow-listed CI/CD actions.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: System integrators consume large dependency ecosystems and may publish packages or use common development tools across many projects. A malicious dependency or development tool can compromise internal builds and become a route to customers. Threat-led context: MITRE v19.2 documents current attacks using compromised packages, CI/CD actions and engineering platforms. Applicability=Core; SupplyChainStage=Supply Chain Compromise; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Developer and AI coding tools can become persistence or propagation points. Altering trusted binaries/configuration can hide malicious execution within normal engineering activity. Applicability: Developer / Build Host. Attack-path stage: Modify Developer / Build Software Binary. Detection opportunities: Binary hash/signature changes; Executable modified outside update process; Tool launching unexpected child processes. Defensive considerations: Code signing; File integrity monitoring; Immutable build images; Trusted software distribution.

data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Use legitimate software deployment, package publishing or endpoint-management tooling to distribute malicious or modified content. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: System integrators and MSPs may possess trusted deployment channels to internal or customer systems. Once CI/CD or release administration is compromised, these mechanisms can amplify the blast radius dramatically. Applicability: Core / Managed Software Delivery. Software supply-chain stage: Abuse Deployment / Release Tooling. Primary assets at risk: Deployment platforms, Release management, Package publishing, RMM/software distribution, Customer deployment tools. Attack-path stage: Abuse Deployment / Release Tooling. Detection opportunities: Mass deployment outside change window; New package/release publisher; Unexpected scripts distributed through trusted platform. Defensive considerations: Four-eyes approval; Signed packages; Change-management correlation; Separate build and deployment privilege.

data.Name: TP-05 | Ingress Tool Transfer
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Download attacker tooling or second-stage payloads into a developer host, runner or build environment. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Malicious workflows commonly retrieve additional code at execution time, reducing the malicious content visible in the repository itself. Detection opportunities: curl/wget/Invoke-WebRequest to new domains; Build jobs downloading unpinned binaries; Unexpected external binary transfer. Defensive considerations: Egress allow-listing for runners; Dependency proxy; Pin downloads by digest; Network monitoring.

Defensive considerations: No privileged runners; Dedicated build accounts; Short sudo cache; EDR.

data.Name: TP-05 | Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-05 Software Supply Chain / Source Code / CI-CD Compromise
data.Description: Add attacker-controlled credentials or certificates to DevOps applications, service principals, service connections or automation identities. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This can create a durable machine-to-machine backdoor into cloud deployments even after the compromised developer account is reset. Applicability: Core / Cloud. Software supply-chain stage: Add Application / Service Principal Credential. Primary assets at risk: Service principals, Service connections, App registrations, Automation accounts. Attack-path stage: Add Application / Service Principal Credential. Detection opportunities: New secret/certificate; Service connection credential change; Credential addition after suspicious repo access. Defensive considerations: Workload identity federation; Managed identities; Restrict credential admins; Alert on new credentials.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: This can create a durable machine-to-machine backdoor into cloud deployments even after the compromised developer account is reset. Threat-led context: No actor-specific evidence required for inclusion; technique is included because it is structurally relevant to the scenario. Applicability=Core / Cloud; SupplyChainStage=Add Application / Service Principal Credential; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.

data.Name: TP-05 | Create Account: Cloud Account

data.Description: Create a new account in a repository, DevOps or cloud environment and grant it project or administrative access. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A new identity can preserve source-control and release access after the original developer account is disabled. Applicability: Cloud DevOps. Software supply-chain stage: Create DevOps / Cloud Backdoor Account. Primary assets at risk: Git services, Azure DevOps, Cloud tenant, Package registries. Attack-path stage: Create DevOps / Cloud Backdoor Account. Detection opportunities: New account outside provisioning flow; Account immediately added to privileged project/group. Defensive considerations: SCIM/central lifecycle governance; Approval; Alert on admin/project account creation.

Defensive considerations: App allow-listing; Admin consent workflow; Least scopes; Periodic app review.

data.Description: Create or modify a systemd service to maintain access on Linux developer or self-hosted runner systems. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Persistent self-hosted runners can become durable attack infrastructure inside the development network. Applicability: Linux Developer / Runner. Software supply-chain stage: Persist on Linux Build / Developer Host. Primary assets at risk: Linux build servers, Self-hosted runners, Developer hosts. Attack-path stage: Persist on Linux Build / Developer Host. Detection opportunities: New systemd service; Service executable in user/temp paths. Defensive considerations: Ephemeral runners; FIM; EDR.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-05 | Generic System Integrator / MSP software-supply-chain profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Persistent self-hosted runners can become durable attack infrastructure inside the development network. Threat-led context: No actor-specific evidence required for inclusion; technique is included because it is structurally relevant to the scenario. Applicability=Linux Developer / Runner; SupplyChainStage=Persist on Linux Build / Developer Host; Priority=Medium; Confidence=Medium. Scope boundary: TP-05 models compromise of developer identities, code repositories, CI/CD platforms and runners, package/dependency ecosystems, artifact/release processes, service connections, secrets, signing/authentication material and trusted software distribution. It includes both attacks against the organisation's development environment and abuse of that environment to compromise downstream customers. Generic identity compromise is covered in TP-01/TP-04, customer-side operations after malicious software reaches a customer belong to TP-03/TP-06, and full data-theft/exfiltration operations are expanded in TP-09. Conditional platform-specific records should be filtered against the actual development stack. This entry is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior has occurred.
