data.Name: TP-08 | Cloud Service Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Enumerate cloud services reachable through a compromised workload or stolen service identity. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A public cloud workload may have access to storage, databases, secrets, messaging or management services. Applicability: Cloud. Internet-facing compromise phase: Discover Cloud Services Available to Workload. Primary assets at risk: Azure services, Cloud storage, Databases, Secrets. Detection opportunities: Rapid service enumeration by workload identity. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; Behavior analytics.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: A public cloud workload may have access to storage, databases, secrets, messaging or management services. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Cloud; Phase=Discover Cloud Services Available to Workload; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Cloud Storage Object Discovery
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: List files and objects in storage accessible to the public-facing application. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Internet-facing applications often hold direct data-store permissions, making object discovery an immediate post-exploit data-access route. Applicability: Cloud. Internet-facing compromise phase: Enumerate Cloud Storage Objects. Primary assets at risk: Object storage, Blobs, Application files, Backups. Detection opportunities: Mass listing after service compromise. Defensive considerations: Per-application storage scope; Monitor unusual enumeration.

data.Name: TP-08 | Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Use recovered credentials to access internal Windows servers or jump hosts over RDP. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: RDP provides interactive administrative access once credentials are recovered from the edge/application foothold. Applicability: Windows. Internet-facing compromise phase: Pivot via RDP. Primary assets at risk: Windows servers, Jump hosts. Detection opportunities: RDP from web/DMZ host or unusual admin source. Defensive considerations: RDP gateway; MFA; Segmentation.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: RDP provides interactive administrative access once credentials are recovered from the edge/application foothold. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Windows; Phase=Pivot via RDP; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Proxy: Internal Proxy
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Use the compromised edge/web server as a SOCKS or port-forwarding proxy into internal networks. data.Description: Name malicious files, services or binaries to resemble legitimate application or system components. data.Name: TP-08 | Disable or Modify System Firewall

data.Description: Disable or modify firewall rules to expose management services, allow C2 or enable lateral movement. Detection opportunities: Firewall rule/config change from new admin/session; New external management rule. Defensive considerations: Config integrity; MFA; Change approval; Out-of-band config backup.

data.Name: TP-08 | Data from Local System
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Collect local configuration, logs, application data, customer files or cached exports from the compromised host. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Internet-facing systems may contain customer tickets, project uploads, configuration and local caches useful for data theft or deeper access. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Collect Data from Public Application Host. Primary assets at risk: Application files, Uploads, Logs, Config. Detection opportunities: Mass file reads; Archive creation. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; DLP; Minimise local sensitive data.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Description: Access objects and files in cloud storage using the application's managed identity, API keys or stolen user credentials. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Cloud-hosted applications often rely on object storage for uploads, documents and backups; excessive permissions can expose large datasets. Applicability: Cloud. Internet-facing compromise phase: Read Cloud Storage Used by Public Service. Primary assets at risk: Azure Storage, Object storage, Uploads, Backups. Detection opportunities: Mass object reads/downloads; New client using workload token. Defensive considerations: Per-app storage scope; Private endpoints; DLP; Versioning.

data.Name: TP-08 | Automated Collection
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Automatically collect application files, database exports, secrets and reachable internal data. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Automation lets attackers harvest data quickly before defenders patch or isolate the vulnerable service. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Automate Public-Service / Backend Data Collection. Primary assets at risk: Application data, Database, Files, Secrets. Detection opportunities: High-volume scripted reads; Recursive collection after exploit. Defensive considerations: DLP; Behavior analytics.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Automation lets attackers harvest data quickly before defenders patch or isolate the vulnerable service. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Core; Phase=Automate Public-Service / Backend Data Collection; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Upload stolen data to attacker-controlled cloud storage or file-sharing services. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Internet-facing servers normally have outbound web access, making cloud-storage exfiltration easy to blend with application traffic. Applicability: Core. Internet-facing compromise phase: Exfiltrate via Cloud Storage. Primary assets at risk: Customer data, Application data, Archives. Detection opportunities: Large upload to new storage service; Rclone/AzCopy from server. Defensive considerations: Egress control; DLP/CASB.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Internet-facing servers normally have outbound web access, making cloud-storage exfiltration easy to blend with application traffic. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Core; Phase=Exfiltrate via Cloud Storage; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-08 | Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-08 Internet-Facing Services Compromise
data.Description: Exploit an application or system weakness to crash, exhaust or deny availability of an internet-facing service. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Even when confidentiality compromise is the main concern, exposed project/support/VPN services may also be disrupted through exploit-driven denial of service. Applicability: Public Service. Internet-facing compromise phase: Impact. Primary assets at risk: VPN, Portal, API, Public application. Detection opportunities: Crash/resource exhaustion correlated with exploit traffic. Defensive considerations: HA; Rate limiting; Patching; WAF.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-08 | Generic System Integrator / MSP internet-facing-services profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Even when confidentiality compromise is the main concern, exposed project/support/VPN services may also be disrupted through exploit-driven denial of service. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to compromise of internet-facing services. Applicability=Public Service; Phase=Impact; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-08 models external reconnaissance, attack-surface discovery, exploitation of public-facing applications and edge appliances, abuse of VPN/remote access and valid public-service accounts, post-exploit command execution, web shell/server persistence, credential and token theft, privilege escalation, internal/cloud discovery, tunneling, lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and selected service-impact actions. It is deliberately generic enough for VPNs, firewalls, web apps, APIs, project portals, Jira/Confluence-like platforms, service desks, RMM gateways and custom customer-facing applications. Product-specific CVEs are evidence/examples, not hard-coded requirements. Identity-only compromise is deeper in TP-01, trusted customer pivot in TP-03, privileged access in TP-04, software supply chain in TP-05, ransomware/destruction in TP-06 and data-theft depth in TP-09. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence that the behavior occurred in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-09 | Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Acquire leaked, stolen or infostealer-derived credentials for SaaS users, administrators and customer-facing personnel. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: SaaS data-theft operations are identity-centric. Stolen credentials can provide immediate access to CRM, M365, ticketing, source repositories and cloud storage. Applicability: Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Targeting. Primary assets at risk: SSO credentials, SaaS administrators, Customer-facing users. Detection opportunities: Leaked credential monitoring; Risk detections. Defensive considerations: Phishing-resistant MFA; Credential exposure response.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: SaaS data-theft operations are identity-centric. Stolen credentials can provide immediate access to CRM, M365, ticketing, source repositories and cloud storage. Threat-led context: M-Trends 2026 highlights identity, OAuth token and SaaS compromise as major data-theft paths. Applicability=Core; Phase=Targeting; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. It covers SSO/session/OAuth compromise, malicious connected applications, CRM, Microsoft 365, messaging, code repositories, databases, cloud storage, support/ticketing data, programmatic API collection, native cloud sharing and data-theft extortion. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Description: Map customers, suppliers, SaaS providers, implementation partners and connected business applications. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: System integrators hold information about many downstream customers and use many interconnected SaaS applications, increasing the value of relationship mapping. Applicability: System Integrator Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Targeting. Primary assets at risk: Customers, Suppliers, SaaS vendors, Connected apps. Detection opportunities: Third-party exposure reviews. Defensive considerations: Vendor governance; Least privilege integrations.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: System integrators hold information about many downstream customers and use many interconnected SaaS applications, increasing the value of relationship mapping. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to SaaS-centric data theft and extortion. Applicability=System Integrator Core; Phase=Targeting; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. data.Name: TP-09 | Phishing: Spearphishing Voice
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Use a phone call to cause the victim to authenticate, approve MFA or authorize a connected application. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is directly demonstrated by current Salesforce data-theft campaigns. Applicability: Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Initial Access. Primary assets at risk: CRM, SSO, Connected apps. Detection opportunities: Authentication changes during call. Defensive considerations: Verified support procedures.

Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to SaaS-centric data theft and extortion. Applicability=Core; Phase=Initial Access; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-09 | Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Use a valid compromised cloud/SaaS identity to access business applications and data. Detection opportunities: SigninLogs; Rare location/device; High-volume exports. Defensive considerations: MFA; Conditional Access; Least privilege.

data.Name: TP-09 | Brute Force: Password Spraying

data.Description: Attempt common passwords across many cloud identities. data.Name: TP-09 | Brute Force: Credential Stuffing
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Use known breached credentials against cloud applications and SSO. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Credential reuse can directly expose SaaS data stores without malware. Applicability: Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Credential Acquisition. Primary assets at risk: SSO, CRM, Support platforms. Detection opportunities: Leaked credential detections. Defensive considerations: MFA; Unique passwords.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to SaaS-centric data theft and extortion. Applicability=Core; Phase=Credential Acquisition; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Description: Steal OAuth tokens, personal access tokens or connected-application tokens. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: OAuth and API tokens can provide long-lived programmatic access and can survive password changes. Applicability: Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Token Theft. Primary assets at risk: OAuth tokens, PATs, Connected app tokens, API tokens. Detection opportunities: Token use from unusual client/IP. Defensive considerations: Short-lived tokens; Token scoping; Rotation.

data.Name: TP-09 | Browser Session Hijacking
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Hijack or replay a browser session to act as the victim in SaaS platforms. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Session hijacking is particularly valuable for SaaS applications where no endpoint foothold is required after the session is acquired. Applicability: Core. data.Name: TP-09 | Cloud Application Integration
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Create or authorize a malicious OAuth/connected application with access to SaaS data. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is one of the defining TP-09 techniques. Connected-app authorization can grant persistent API access independent of the victim's interactive session. Applicability: SaaS Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Application Persistence. Primary assets at risk: Salesforce connected apps, OAuth apps, M365 app registrations. Detection opportunities: New app authorization; High-risk scopes; Unusual connected app. Defensive considerations: Admin consent workflow; App governance; Least scopes.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: This is one of the defining TP-09 techniques. Connected-app authorization can grant persistent API access independent of the victim's interactive session. Threat-led context: Salesforce Data Exfiltration campaign used malicious connected apps / modified Data Loader. Applicability=SaaS Core; Phase=Application Persistence; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. It covers SSO/session/OAuth compromise, malicious connected applications, CRM, Microsoft 365, messaging, code repositories, databases, cloud storage, support/ticketing data, programmatic API collection, native cloud sharing and data-theft extortion. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

Defensive considerations: Workload federation; Credential-change alerts.

data.Name: TP-09 | Modify Authentication Process: Conditional Access Policies
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Modify access policies or exclusions to permit attacker-controlled sessions. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A privileged cloud identity can weaken controls across all connected SaaS applications. Applicability: Privileged Identity. SaaS data-theft phase: Persistence. Primary assets at risk: Conditional Access, Trusted locations. Detection opportunities: Policy changes; New exclusions. Defensive considerations: PIM; Alert on policy changes.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: A privileged cloud identity can weaken controls across all connected SaaS applications. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to SaaS-centric data theft and extortion. Applicability=Privileged Identity; Phase=Persistence; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. It covers SSO/session/OAuth compromise, malicious connected applications, CRM, Microsoft 365, messaging, code repositories, databases, cloud storage, support/ticketing data, programmatic API collection, native cloud sharing and data-theft extortion. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-09 | Cloud Service Dashboard
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Use legitimate SaaS dashboards to inspect data, users, permissions, integrations and export functions. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Interactive access through normal dashboards can blend with legitimate administration. Applicability: Core. SaaS data-theft phase: SaaS Discovery. Primary assets at risk: CRM admin, M365 admin, Support platform admin. Detection opportunities: Portal access from rare device/location. Defensive considerations: Managed admin devices; PIM.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Interactive access through normal dashboards can blend with legitimate administration. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to SaaS-centric data theft and extortion. Applicability=Core; Phase=SaaS Discovery; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. It covers SSO/session/OAuth compromise, malicious connected applications, CRM, Microsoft 365, messaging, code repositories, databases, cloud storage, support/ticketing data, programmatic API collection, native cloud sharing and data-theft extortion. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to SaaS-centric data theft and extortion. Applicability=M365 Core; Phase=Collection; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. It covers SSO/session/OAuth compromise, malicious connected applications, CRM, Microsoft 365, messaging, code repositories, databases, cloud storage, support/ticketing data, programmatic API collection, native cloud sharing and data-theft extortion. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Description: Mine Confluence or equivalent knowledge repositories for customer, architecture, credential and operational information. data.Name: TP-09 | Data from Information Repositories: Customer Relationship Management Software
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Access and export CRM records such as PII, customer contacts, support details, account history and commercial data. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: CRM is one of the most relevant SaaS data-theft targets for system integrators because it combines customer relationships with rich business context. Applicability: CRM Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Collection. Primary assets at risk: Salesforce, Dynamics 365, HubSpot, Zendesk-like CRM. Detection opportunities: High-volume CRM access/export; Rare user reading PII. Defensive considerations: Least privilege; Export controls; DLP.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: CRM is one of the most relevant SaaS data-theft targets for system integrators because it combines customer relationships with rich business context. Threat-led context: ATT&CK C0059 and ShinyHunters map directly to large-scale CRM/Salesforce data collection. Applicability=CRM Core; Phase=Collection; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. It covers SSO/session/OAuth compromise, malicious connected applications, CRM, Microsoft 365, messaging, code repositories, databases, cloud storage, support/ticketing data, programmatic API collection, native cloud sharing and data-theft extortion. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-09 | Data from Information Repositories: Databases
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Query or export data from SaaS and cloud databases such as Snowflake, Azure SQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB or other repositories. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Database theft can expose large volumes of PII, financial, credential and customer data and is directly associated with extortion campaigns. Applicability: Database Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Collection. Primary assets at risk: Snowflake, Azure SQL, Cloud databases, Application databases. Detection opportunities: Bulk query/export; Rare identity exporting large datasets. Defensive considerations: DB least privilege; MFA where supported; Query/export monitoring.

data.Name: TP-09 | Data from Cloud Storage
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Read and download data from cloud storage using compromised identities or application tokens. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Cloud storage frequently contains project, customer, backup and user files and can be accessed entirely through legitimate APIs. Applicability: Cloud Storage Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Collection. Primary assets at risk: OneDrive, Azure Storage, S3-like object storage. Detection opportunities: Mass download; Unusual API client. Defensive considerations: DLP; Storage least privilege; Versioning.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. data.Description: Search documents, repositories, tickets and exports for credentials, API keys and secrets. data.Name: TP-09 | Credentials from Password Stores: Cloud Secrets Management Stores
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Use stolen cloud privilege to retrieve secrets from Azure Key Vault or equivalent. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Secret-store access can transform SaaS data theft into persistent application/customer access. Applicability: Cloud. SaaS data-theft phase: Credential Expansion. Primary assets at risk: Cloud secret stores, Service credentials. Detection opportunities: Bulk secret reads. Defensive considerations: PIM; Managed identity least privilege.

Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to SaaS-centric data theft and extortion. Applicability=Core; Phase=Staging; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. It covers SSO/session/OAuth compromise, malicious connected applications, CRM, Microsoft 365, messaging, code repositories, databases, cloud storage, support/ticketing data, programmatic API collection, native cloud sharing and data-theft extortion. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-09 | Automated Exfiltration
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Automatically export and transfer SaaS data through APIs or scripted tooling. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: ATT&CK C0059 maps Salesforce data theft directly to Automated Exfiltration. Applicability: Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Exfiltration. Primary assets at risk: CRM exports, Cloud files, Database records. Detection opportunities: High-rate automated export; API pagination at unusual scale. Defensive considerations: API rate/behavior controls; DLP.

data.Name: TP-09 | Data Transfer Size Limits
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Break large exports into smaller chunks to avoid limits or detection thresholds. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Chunking can make high-volume data theft less obvious and work around SaaS/API transfer limits. Applicability: Conditional. SaaS data-theft phase: Exfiltration. Primary assets at risk: Export archives, API data. Detection opportunities: Repeated fixed-size transfers. Defensive considerations: Behavioral volume analytics.

data.Name: TP-09 | Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Transfer stolen SaaS data through an existing C2 or attacker-controlled HTTPS channel. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Where SaaS collection is performed by an endpoint script or malware, the same channel can carry exfiltrated content. Applicability: Endpoint / Scripted. SaaS data-theft phase: Exfiltration. Primary assets at risk: SaaS exports, Files. Detection opportunities: Large outbound transfer by C2 process. Defensive considerations: Egress monitoring; DLP.

data.Name: TP-09 | Exfiltration Over Web Service
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Use legitimate web-service APIs to export stolen data. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This is central to SaaS data theft: the exfiltration can occur through the same legitimate Salesforce, Microsoft or cloud API used by normal users. Applicability: Core. SaaS data-theft phase: Exfiltration. Primary assets at risk: Salesforce API, Graph API, Cloud APIs. Detection opportunities: Unusual export/API volume. Defensive considerations: DLP; API behavior analytics.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: This is central to SaaS data theft: the exfiltration can occur through the same legitimate Salesforce, Microsoft or cloud API used by normal users. Threat-led context: Salesforce Data Exfiltration used legitimate Salesforce API communications for exfiltration. Applicability=Core; Phase=Exfiltration; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. It covers SSO/session/OAuth compromise, malicious connected applications, CRM, Microsoft 365, messaging, code repositories, databases, cloud storage, support/ticketing data, programmatic API collection, native cloud sharing and data-theft extortion. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-09 | Transfer Data to Cloud Account
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Use native cloud sharing, ownership transfer, sync, snapshot copy or anonymous links to move data to an attacker-controlled account in the same or another cloud service context. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This can bypass network-centric exfiltration monitoring because the transfer occurs inside legitimate cloud-provider APIs. Applicability: Cloud Native. SaaS data-theft phase: Exfiltration. Primary assets at risk: OneDrive, SharePoint, Cloud storage, Snapshots. Detection opportunities: External sharing; SAS/anonymous link creation; Cross-account transfer. Defensive considerations: External sharing restrictions; DLP; Sharing alerts.

data.Name: TP-09 | Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Cloud Log
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-09 SaaS / Data Exfiltration / Data-Theft Extortion
data.Description: Disable or alter SaaS/cloud logging, audit export or SIEM integration. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A privileged SaaS attacker can reduce visibility before bulk collection or extortion. Applicability: Privileged SaaS. SaaS data-theft phase: Defense Impairment. Primary assets at risk: SaaS audit, Cloud logs, SIEM export. Detection opportunities: Audit setting changes; Ingestion gaps. Defensive considerations: Separate log administration; Protected log export.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-09 | Generic System Integrator / MSP SaaS data-theft and extortion profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to SaaS-centric data theft and extortion. Applicability=Privileged SaaS; Phase=Defense Impairment; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-09 models cloud/SaaS data theft where the principal objective is access to, collection of and exfiltration of data rather than endpoint encryption. Generic phishing belongs to TP-07, ransomware/destructive encryption to TP-06, and supplier-side compromise to TP-10, though techniques are intentionally cross-referenced. data.Description: Identify customers, suppliers, MSPs, SaaS vendors, cloud partners, resellers, managed-service providers and technology dependencies that possess trusted access or sensitive information. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Third-party compromise is impossible to model without understanding who trusts whom. System integrators sit in dense trust graphs and may both consume privileged supplier services and hold privileged access into downstream customers. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Trust Mapping. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Supplier relationships, Customer relationships, MSP contracts, SaaS integrations, Cloud partner relationships. Detection opportunities: Third-party inventory review; Attack-surface correlation; Unexpected vendor/customer identity activity. Defensive considerations: Maintain authoritative third-party trust inventory; Classify access type and privilege; Review trust at onboarding/offboarding.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Third-party compromise is impossible to model without understanding who trusts whom. System integrators sit in dense trust graphs and may both consume privileged supplier services and hold privileged access into downstream customers. Threat-led context: ATT&CK T1199 explicitly models abuse of organisations that already have access to intended victims. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Core; Phase=Trust Mapping; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. It covers supplier/MSP/customer identities, vendor VPN and remote support, RMM, SaaS/OAuth/PAT integrations, delegated cloud access, software/dependency/hardware supply chains, code repositories and service connections, cross-boundary lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and destructive/ransomware follow-on. Both inbound Supplierâ†’Organisation and outbound Organisationâ†’Customer paths are included because a system integrator may be victim and stepping stone simultaneously. TP-02/TP-03 provide deeper Microsoft partner/customer pivot coverage; TP-05 deeper CI/CD supply-chain detail; TP-09 deeper SaaS data theft. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-10 | Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Identify staff and external contacts responsible for vendor management, support, managed services, remote access, SaaS administration and customer administration. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Role discovery helps attackers target identities that can approve support access, reset credentials, authorize integrations or move between organisations. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Trust Mapping. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Vendor managers, Support engineers, Customer admins, MSP operators, SaaS admins. Detection opportunities: Targeting intelligence; Role-based phishing patterns. Defensive considerations: Separate privileged identities; Strong vendor verification; Least privilege.

data.Name: TP-10 | Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Obtain credentials belonging to supplier administrators, MSP operators, customer support accounts, external consultants or integration identities. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Credentials associated with third parties often have legitimate remote or SaaS access and may receive less scrutiny than internal administrator accounts. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Targeting. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Vendor accounts, Customer support accounts, MSP identities, Guest/B2B users, Service accounts. Detection opportunities: Leaked credential monitoring; Third-party risky-signin correlation. Defensive considerations: MFA; Named accounts; Rapid credential revocation; No shared vendor accounts.

data.Name: TP-10 | External Remote Services
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Authenticate through VPN, Citrix, vendor portals or other remote-access services granted to suppliers/MSPs/customers. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Third-party remote access is a direct entry path and is explicitly called out by CISA guidance for MSP/customer environments. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Trusted Entry. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Vendor VPN, Customer VPN, Citrix, Remote support gateways. Detection opportunities: New source/device for third-party account; Remote access outside maintenance window. Defensive considerations: MFA; Named users; Time-bound enablement; Source restrictions; Session recording.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Third-party remote access is a direct entry path and is explicitly called out by CISA guidance for MSP/customer environments. Threat-led context: CISA recommends auditing third-party remote access and publicly accessible RMM/MSP accounts. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Core; Phase=Trusted Entry; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. It covers supplier/MSP/customer identities, vendor VPN and remote support, RMM, SaaS/OAuth/PAT integrations, delegated cloud access, software/dependency/hardware supply chains, code repositories and service connections, cross-boundary lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and destructive/ransomware follow-on. Both inbound Supplierâ†’Organisation and outbound Organisationâ†’Customer paths are included because a system integrator may be victim and stepping stone simultaneously. TP-02/TP-03 provide deeper Microsoft partner/customer pivot coverage; TP-05 deeper CI/CD supply-chain detail; TP-09 deeper SaaS data theft. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-10 | Remote Access Tools: Remote Desktop Software
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Use legitimate remote monitoring and management or remote desktop software to access downstream systems. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: RMM tools are a uniquely important third-party risk because one management platform can reach many endpoints or customers and is often trusted/allow-listed. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: MSP / Support Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Trusted Remote Administration. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: RMM console, Remote support agents, Managed endpoints, Customer servers. Detection opportunities: Unexpected RMM operator/source; Mass sessions; Access outside ticket/change window. Defensive considerations: MFA; Named operators; Session recording; Approval/ticket correlation; Restrict unattended access.

data.Description: Replay a stolen third-party session to operate inside the trusted application or customer environment. Third-party lifecycle phase: Replay Trusted Third-Party Session. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: SaaS, Partner portal, Customer portal. Detection opportunities: New IP/device for same session. Defensive considerations: Rapid revocation; Session binding.

data.Description: Grant additional roles to supplier/customer identities or integration principals. data.Name: TP-10 | Software Deployment Tools
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Use software deployment, RMM, package deployment or update tooling to distribute attacker-controlled software to trusted systems. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Deployment platforms multiply blast radius because one management channel can install software across many internal or customer endpoints. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core MSP / Software Delivery. Third-party lifecycle phase: Abuse Trusted Software Deployment Mechanism. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Software deployment, RMM, Package distribution, Update services. Detection opportunities: Mass deployment outside change window; New package/publisher; Unsigned/unexpected payload. Defensive considerations: Separation of duties; Code signing; Approval; Change correlation.

Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Privilege discovery shows whether a trusted account can reach high-value customer or supplier resources. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core Cloud. Third-party lifecycle phase: Discover External / Delegated Cloud Privilege. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Cloud groups, Delegated admin groups, Azure roles. Detection opportunities: Bulk group/role enumeration. Defensive considerations: PIM; Review external group membership.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Privilege discovery shows whether a trusted account can reach high-value customer or supplier resources. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to third-party, supplier, MSP, SaaS integration or customer trust compromise. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Core Cloud; Phase=Discover External / Delegated Cloud Privilege; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. It covers supplier/MSP/customer identities, vendor VPN and remote support, RMM, SaaS/OAuth/PAT integrations, delegated cloud access, software/dependency/hardware supply chains, code repositories and service connections, cross-boundary lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and destructive/ransomware follow-on. Both inbound Supplierâ†’Organisation and outbound Organisationâ†’Customer paths are included because a system integrator may be victim and stepping stone simultaneously. TP-02/TP-03 provide deeper Microsoft partner/customer pivot coverage; TP-05 deeper CI/CD supply-chain detail; TP-09 deeper SaaS data theft. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

Defensive considerations: Least privilege; Behavior analytics.

data.Description: Delete data or resources accessible through supplier/customer trust. Third-party lifecycle phase: Destroy Data Through Trusted Access. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Customer data, Cloud resources, Supplier systems. Detection opportunities: Mass delete by external/vendor identity. Defensive considerations: Retention/versioning; Resource locks; Backups.
